transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2025-09-23
- Time: 11:00 AM EDT
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luis (Redwood SE), Rhea (Redwood Product), Priya (Veridian Head of ML), Tom (Eng Manager), Anika (Security), Evan (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto generated, might be incomplete): Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations for batching and prefix/KV caching to reduce per-token costs while meeting P95 latency targets. Some reference links: https://app.redwood.ai/optimize/console (example), cost-sheet-v2.xlsx (shared link, see follow-up email).

[00:00] Maya Chen: All right everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna kick off in a sec. Hi Priya, Tom, Anika, Evan, can you hear me OK?
[00:06] Priya Nair: Yep yep, loud and clear. Thanks, excited to see the playbook.
[00:10] Tom Spencer: Morning.
[00:12] Luis Ortega: Hi team, Luis from Redwood SE. Today we'll do a Optimize walkthrough — the focus is prefetch strategy, batching knobs, and show cost model scenarios. We'll start with your workload and then map recs.
[00:20] Priya Nair: Quick context: our main product is an investment research assistant, ~200k daily active queries, many short prompts (10-50 tokens) but also long context retrievals for deep-dive prompts, sessions are sticky per user. P95 latency target is 500ms for the short prompts, but we tolerate up to 1.5s for long ones. We're currently on a mix of hosted endpoints and some self-hosted instances in GCP, cost is spiking.
[00:38] Maya Chen: Perfect, that helps. Are you doing session KV caching today at all?
[00:42] Priya Nair: We have a naive session cache in-app but it's not integrated with the model KV, so we get very low effective cache hit. Mostly we cache final responses.
[00:52] Luis Ortega: Okay, so there's a big opportunity for prefix/KV prefetch and lookahead. We'll walk through three profiles: conservative prefetch (low memory, minimal extra calls), aggressive prefetch (stores prefixes in KV, higher memory, fewer model tokens), and hybrid sessionization.
[01:10] Tom Spencer: Can you define what you mean by prefetch, like are we proactively calling the model? That worries me from cost perspective if we double model calls.
[01:18] Luis Ortega: Good question. Prefetch here means when you detect a session continuation probability above a threshold, you compute the likely next KV prefix and warm it in the runtime's KV store. It's not a full generation call necessarily — we can cache the KV state so subsequent user tokens reuse the attention cache and don't re-run full layers. In many workloads that reduces tokens generated by 30-60% for follow-ups.
[01:38] Rhea Singh: And we simulate this in the Optimize console — there's a model that estimates hit-rate uplift given your sessionization and the trace. The cost model parameters are: baseline tokens, average batch size, cache hit rate, prefetch ratio, and memory overhead.
[01:52] Priya Nair: So what's the tradeoff exactly? Memory and CPU on the server side vs token costs on the model?
[01:58] Luis Ortega: Exactly. Also latency: if prefetch warms the KV ahead of a user action, p95 drops because there's less generation work in-path. But if you do aggressive prefetch and wrong predictions, you waste memory and may evict useful states.
[02:14] [crosstalk] Evan Brooks: Also need to think about burst capacity — prefetch can create spikes in GPU usage if it happens across many sessions at once.
[02:20] Luis Ortega: Correct, that's why we recommend adaptive backoff and a burst window cap in the runtime. The console has a simulator to run traffic traces and show GPU usage over time.

[02:42] Maya Chen: We'll pull up the Optimize console. I'll share my screen — give me a sec.
[02:47] [screen share noise]
[03:10] Luis Ortega: On the left we've loaded the Veridian sample trace (thanks Priya for the dump). You can see the session affinity matrix, average inter-arrival times, and top prompt families. Over on the right is the prefetchoverlay simulation with three scenarios.
[03:28] Priya Nair: Nice, that session heatmap is helpful. Our long-tail sessions are the costly ones.
[03:34] Luis Ortega: For the cost model, we ran a baseline: no prefix, batching set to 1 (low concurrency), and TTL-based cache only. Baseline per token cost is X (we'll send actual numbers in the sheet). Scenario A — conservative prefetch — minimal memory, expected cache hit uplift 18%, cost reduction ~12% while keeping P95 under 500ms for short prompts. Scenario B — aggressive prefetch — 45% hit uplift, cost reduction ~28%, but memory overhead and peak GPU load increases ~1.6x. Scenario C — hybrid with session pinning: 35% uplift, 22% cost reduction, peak load manageable with autoscale policy.
[04:20] Tom Spencer: The numbers look promising. Are those modeled for a concrete model size? Our prod uses a 13B quantized variant.
[04:26] Luis Ortega: Yes those are for a 13B quantized profile at your observed seq length distribution. If you switch to a larger 70B model the memory/page behavior changes; the console supports plugging different model profiles.
[04:36] Priya Nair: How does batching factor in? We thought batching always saves cost but increases latency.
[04:40] Rhea Singh: Right, batching reduces per-token overhead but introduces queueing latency. We recommend dynamic batching windows keyed by prompt family. For short prompts, use shallow batching (20-40ms window) to keep P95 within 500ms but still get batching benefits. For long prompts you can use larger windows. Optimize suggests per-route batch windows and shows the sensitivity curve.
[04:59] [00:05 pause]
[05:05] Anika Patel: From a security perspective, any caching persists state — is KV stored encrypted and how do you control retention? We have strict requirements for financial data.
[05:12] Luis Ortega: Yes, for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and all KV is encrypted at rest. Retention is policy-driven — you can TTL keys or enforce per-tenant eviction. We also obfuscate PII via pre-processing before caching if needed.
[05:26] Anika Patel: What about audit logs? We need a chain of custody that shows who accessed which session state.
[05:31] Maya Chen: The Redwood console logs token-level events for audit windows, including cache hits/misses, prefetch triggers, and who/which keyspace accessed them. We'll share the SOC 2 + audit log docs.

[05:48] Priya Nair: Back to cost modelling — can we see a sensitivity table for hit rate vs cost saved per million queries?
[05:54] Luis Ortega: Absolutely, the cost sheet computes cost per million queries across varying cache hit rates, batching sizes, and prefetch accuracy. Here's a snippet — assume baseline tokens per query 120, baseline batching 1. If hit rate moves from 10% to 40%, you see non-linear savings because fewer tokens run end-to-end. We'll email the spreadsheet with explicit formulas.
[06:18] Tom Spencer: Is it feasible to A/B test prefetch on a subset of traffic? We want to measure actual hit rate vs predicted before a full rollout.
[06:24] Luis Ortega: Yes, canary is the recommended plan. Redwood's rollout policies allow traffic split by user cohort and automatic rollback if latency regressions exceed thresholds. We can set a 5% cohort to start.

[06:40] [07:00 jump — moderator note: skipped a long demo clip]
[07:05] Luis Ortega: Now showing the simulation chart — X axis is time, Y left is GPU token throughput, Y right is P95 latency. See the spike where aggressive prefetch warmed many sessions; you get peak GPU usage but average cost still lower.
[07:22] Evan Brooks: That spike is concerning for us — we operate under tight capacity constraints. Can the runtime smooth prefetches across a sliding window?
[07:28] Luis Ortega: Yes, we support rate-limited prefetch and randomized jitter to smooth bursts. Also the autoscaler can prioritize core inference traffic and defer background prefetching if needed.

[07:50] Priya Nair: A practical question: how much developer effort to integrate this? We have an existing microservice that talks to several model endpoints.
[07:57] Maya Chen: Integration can be incremental. Option 1 (fastest): use Redwood's SDK with one small middleware that signals session events and lets the runtime manage prefetch decisions. Option 2: full integration where you export session traces to Optimize and adopt the prefetch API. Typical integration time for Option 1 is 2-3 engineering days for a single service.
[08:16] Tom Spencer: For our infra team, we'll need a minimal change list — can you send a short runbook?
[08:21] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll attach a runbook with code snippets and the SDK link.

[08:35] Rhea Singh: Quick demo of the console's ROI slider — when Priya increases the tolerance for TTL and prefetch budget, you can see the cost vs latency tradeoff move in real time.
[08:46] Priya Nair: I like the ROI slider. Does it account for cloud egress or networking costs (we have strict VPC routing)?
[08:52] Luis Ortega: It models compute and token costs primarily. For deployments inside your VPC/on-prem we can plug in your infra costs like egress or cross-region pricing if you provide unit rates. We'll help customize the model for Veridian.

[09:10] Anika Patel: A couple compliance concerns — data residency, KMS separation, and logging retention. Do you allow the control plane in Redwood but data plane fully in our VPC?
[09:18] Maya Chen: Yes, that's the Private deployment pattern — control plane hosted, data plane in your VPC. We also offer full air-gapped on-prem packages for regulated customers. We'll include details in the security packet.

[09:34] [minor audio glitch]
[09:40] Priya Nair: About the canary: what success metrics should we track? Cost delta obviously, but also p95, p99, and error rates?
[09:48] Luis Ortega: Correct — track P95 latency for short prompts, P99 for safety, model error rates (if you have automated evals), cache hit rate, and GPU utilization. We can push these as dashboards into your Grafana or in the Redwood console.

[10:05] Tom Spencer: Any gotchas with quantized models and KV cache? We use int8 quant for 13B.
[10:11] Luis Ortega: Most of our runtime optimizations are quantization-aware. The main gotcha is how attention cache shapes map to quantized kernel tiling — which affects memory footprint. The console's model profiles account for that.

[10:30] Maya Chen: Let's summarize and agree on next steps.
[10:33] Maya Chen: Action items: Maya will send cost spreadsheet, Rhea will attach runbook and security packet, Luis will schedule sandbox benchmark, Priya to share traces. Anything to add?
[10:44] Priya Nair: Also please include an example canary config and the rollout SLO thresholds.
[10:48] Maya Chen: Will do.

[11:00] [wrap]
[11:02] Tom Spencer: Great session, thanks everyone.
[11:04] Anika Patel: Thanks.
[11:06] Luis Ortega: Thanks team, we'll follow up with the links.
